question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

EXACERBATE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Aggravate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Exacerbate (verb) means to make a problem, illness or bad situation worse. (बिगाड़ना, और गंभीर बनाना)
◦ Example: The sudden withdrawal of subsidies exacerbated the farmers’ distress.

 

• Aggravate carries exactly the same sense — to intensify or worsen something already unpleasant. (गंभीर बनाना)
◦ Example: Lifting the heavy crate aggravated his old back injury.

 

• Note that the word applies only to something already bad. One may exacerbate a shortage or a quarrel, but never a success.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Alleviate (कम करना, राहत देना): to make suffering or a problem less severe — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 3: Soothe (शांत करना): to calm or relieve — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Mitigate (नरम करना, घटाना): to lessen the seriousness of something — again the reverse of exacerbate. Candidates often confuse mitigate with exacerbate; they are opposites.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of exacerbate asked in SSC: worsen, inflame, compound, intensify, heighten.

 

• Antonyms: assuage, ameliorate, appease, relieve, palliate.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

EXONERATE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Incriminate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Exonerate (verb) means to declare somebody free from blame or from a charge. (दोषमुक्त करना)
◦ Example: The inquiry exonerated the officer of every allegation.

 

• Incriminate means to make somebody appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing, and is therefore its direct opposite. (दोषी ठहराना, फँसाना)
◦ Example: The recovered messages incriminated two of the accused.

 

• The word comes from Latin ex- (out of) + onus (burden) — literally “to take the burden off”. The same root gives onerous (burdensome).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Acquit (बरी करना): to declare not guilty in a court of law — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Absolve (मुक्त करना): to free from guilt or obligation — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Exculpate (निर्दोष सिद्ध करना): to clear from a charge of fault — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Three options agree and one stands apart — the odd option is the answer. Other antonyms of exonerate: convict, accuse, indict, implicate, condemn.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To let the cat out of the bag
option_1: To reveal a secret carelessly or unintentionally
option_2: To set free something that was safely confined
option_3: To create panic over an imaginary danger
option_4: To make an expensive mistake in business
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To reveal a secret carelessly or unintentionally.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To let the cat out of the bag” means to disclose a secret, usually by accident or carelessness. (भेद खोल देना, राज़ खोलना)
◦ Example: He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise transfer before the order was issued.

 

• The expression is traced to old market fraud, in which a buyer who had paid for a suckling pig discovered, on opening the sack, that a cat had been substituted for it.

 

• Note that the disclosure is unintended or thoughtless; a deliberate disclosure would be “to blow the whistle” or “to spill the beans” in a planned sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the idiom literally, which is precisely the trap in idiom questions.

 

• Option 3 describes raising a false alarm — “to cry wolf”.

 

• Option 4 describes a costly error — “to pay through the nose” or “to burn one’s fingers”.

 

NOTE

 

• Cat idioms tested by SSC: to bell the cat (to undertake a risky task), a cat-and-dog life (constant quarrelling), to rain cats and dogs (to rain heavily), not room to swing a cat (very cramped).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

OBDURATE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Yielding.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Obdurate (adjective) means stubbornly refusing to change one’s opinion or course of action, and unmoved by persuasion or pity. (हठी, अडिग)
◦ Example: The management remained obdurate despite three rounds of talks.

 

• Yielding means willing to give way, compliant and flexible, and is therefore its direct opposite. (नम्र, समझौता करने वाला)
◦ Example: A more yielding negotiator would have settled the dispute in a day.

 

• The word comes from Latin obdurare (to harden), from durus — hard — the same root as durable and endure.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Stubborn (जिद्दी): refusing to change one’s mind — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Inflexible (अडिग, कठोर): unwilling to alter a position — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Adamant (अटल): absolutely determined not to change — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of obdurate: pliable, tractable, amenable, docile, relenting. Related synonyms often asked: intransigent, obstinate, recalcitrant, dogged.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the scientific study of earthquakes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Seismology.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Seismology is the branch of science that deals with earthquakes and the movement of waves through the earth. (भूकंप विज्ञान)
◦ Example: Advances in seismology have improved the early warning systems along the fault line.

 

• The spelling follows the Greek root seismos (a shaking), so the word begins s-e-i-s-, with the ‘e’ before the ‘i’, and ends with the usual -logy (study of), which has a single l.

 

• The same root gives seismic, seismograph (the recording instrument) and seismometer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Siesmology — the ‘i’ and ‘e’ have been transposed; this is the commonest error with the word.

 

• Option 3: Seizmology — a ‘z’ wrongly replaces the second ‘s’ of seismos.

 

• Option 4: Seismollogy — the suffix -logy has been given a double ‘l’.

 

NOTE

 

• Branches of science whose spellings recur in SSC: entomology (insects), etymology (word origins), ornithology (birds), pathology (disease), numismatics (coins), philately (stamps).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitution for:

 ‘The formal act of giving up a throne or high office’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Abdication.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abdication means the formal renunciation of a throne or of sovereign power by the person who holds it. (राज्यत्याग, पदत्याग)
◦ Example: The abdication of the king in 1936 startled the whole empire.

 

• It is formed from Latin ab- (away) + dicare (to proclaim) — literally to renounce publicly. The essential idea is that the ruler gives up power voluntarily.

 

• The word is also used figuratively for the giving up of a duty — an abdication of responsibility.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Resignation (इस्तीफा): the giving up of an ordinary office or job — correct in general use, but not the word reserved for a throne.

 

• Option 3: Secession (अलगाव, पृथक्करण): the formal withdrawal of a region or group from a larger political union.

 

• Option 4: Deposition (पदच्युति): the removal of a ruler by others — the opposite of a voluntary surrender of power.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish the cluster carefully: abdication (giving up willingly), deposition/dethronement (removed by force), usurpation (seizing power unlawfully), regency (rule on behalf of a minor), interregnum (a gap between two reigns).

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: ‘A word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Anagram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An anagram is a word or phrase made by rearranging all the letters of another word or phrase. (वर्णविन्यास बदलकर बना शब्द)
◦ Example: ‘Listen’ and ‘silent’ are anagrams of each other.

 

• The word comes from Greek ana- (back, again) + gramma (letter) — literally letters written anew.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Acronym (संक्षिप्त शब्द): a word formed from the initial letters of a name or phrase and pronounced as a word — NASA, RADAR, LASER.

 

• Option 3: Palindrome (प्रतिलोम शब्द): a word or sentence that reads the same backwards and forwards — level, madam, civic.

 

• Option 4: Acrostic: a poem or arrangement in which the first letters of successive lines spell out a word or message.

 

NOTE

 

• Related word-play terms worth revising: pseudonym (an assumed name), synonym (same meaning), homonym (same spelling, different meaning), eponym (a person after whom something is named), portmanteau (a word blending two others, as brunch).

question:
Choose the correct phrasal verb:

 

Despite the mounting criticism, the minister refused to ____ his earlier assurance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. go back on.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ‘To go back on’ means to fail to keep a promise, agreement or assurance. (वचन से मुकरना)
◦ Complete sentence: Despite the mounting criticism, the minister refused to go back on his earlier assurance.
◦ Example: A government that goes back on its word loses the confidence of the market.

 

• The sentence supplies two clues. The object is an assurance, which is something one either keeps or breaks; and the contrast set up by “Despite the mounting criticism … refused to” shows that the minister stood firm — he declined to break his word.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘go along with’ means to agree with or accept a proposal — He went along with the committee’s view.

 

• Option 3: ‘go through with’ means to complete something difficult that one has begun — She went through with the operation.

 

• Option 4: ‘go down with’ means to fall ill with a disease — He went down with a fever.

 

NOTE

 

• Phrasal verbs on go appear repeatedly in SSC: go over (to examine), go for (to choose or attack), go off (to explode; of food, to spoil), go on (to continue), go in for (to take up as a pursuit).

question:
Select the correct option:

 

The report was valued not so much for its length as for the ____ with which every claim in it had been verified.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. rigour.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The construction ‘not so much X as Y’ means that Y matters more than X. The blank must therefore name the quality for which the report was really admired — and the clause that follows explains it: every claim had been verified.

 

• Rigour (noun) means strictness, thoroughness and exactness in method or judgement. (कठोरता, सूक्ष्मता)
◦ Example: The findings survived scrutiny because of the rigour of the sampling.

 

• Note how the sentence is built: verification is a matter of care and discipline, so only a word denoting thoroughness can complete it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Levity (हल्कापन): a light-hearted or frivolous treatment of a serious matter — the reverse of what verification demands.

 

• Option 3: Brevity (संक्षिप्तता): shortness of expression; it would contradict the reference to length rather than complete the contrast.

 

• Option 4: Haste (जल्दबाजी): hurry — the opposite of careful verification.

 

NOTE

 

• Structures that decide such blanks: not so much … as, less … than, rather than, more … than. In each, the element after the second word is the one the writer endorses.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The senior counsel offered me (1)/ a valuable advice (2)/ which I could not afford (3)/ to ignore at that stage. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Advice is an uncountable noun. It therefore takes no article ‘a/an’ and has no plural form. The correct expression is ‘a valuable piece of advice’ or simply ‘valuable advice’.
◦ Corrected: The senior counsel offered me valuable advice which I could not afford to ignore at that stage.

 

• Uncountable nouns are quantified by phrases such as a piece of, an item of, a bit of, a great deal of, much — never by a/an, many or the plural -s.

 

• Do not confuse the noun advice (सलाह) with the verb advise (सलाह देना), which is spelt with an s.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: offered me takes an indirect object without any preposition.

 

• Part (3) is correct: could not afford is well formed.

 

• Part (4) is correct: to ignore at that stage completes the verb afford.

 

NOTE

 

• Common uncountable nouns that SSC tests: advice, information, furniture, luggage, baggage, machinery, scenery, poetry, equipment, stationery, evidence, news, work. None of them takes a/an or a plural -s.

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

The municipality has repaired all the street lights in the ward.
option_1: All the street lights in the ward has been repaired by the municipality.
option_2: All the street lights in the ward have been repaired by the municipality.
option_3: All the street lights in the ward were repaired by the municipality.
option_4: All the street lights in the ward have repaired by the municipality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. All the street lights in the ward have been repaired by the municipality.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active verb has repaired is in the present perfect, whose passive is formed as:
◦ Object + has/have been + V3 + by + subject.

 

• Two points of agreement must be handled together:
◦ the new subject is all the street lights, which is plural, so the auxiliary becomes have been, not has been — the singular has of the active sentence belonged to the municipality;
◦ the main verb takes its third form, repaired, preceded by been.

 

• Passive: All the street lights in the ward have been repaired by the municipality.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the singular has been with a plural subject.

 

• Option 3 shifts the tense to the simple past, altering the time of the action.

 

• Option 4 omits been, leaving an active perfect form with a passive meaning — a very common error.

 

NOTE

 

• In the passive, the auxiliary always agrees with the new subject, never with the original one. He has written the letters → The letters have been written by him.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The general manager, along with his three assistants, (1)/ were present at the meeting (2)/ which had been convened (3)/ to review the annual targets. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is ‘The general manager’, which is singular. The verb must therefore be was present, not were present.
◦ Corrected: The general manager, along with his three assistants, was present at the meeting which had been convened to review the annual targets.

 

• Phrases such as along with, together with, as well as, in addition to, accompanied by, besides, including merely add information; they do not make a singular subject plural. Such a phrase is usually set off by commas — a visual clue that it can be lifted out of the sentence.

 

• Compare with and, which genuinely joins two subjects: The general manager and his assistants were present.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: the parenthetical phrase is properly punctuated with commas.

 

• Part (3) is correct: the past perfect passive had been convened rightly marks the earlier action.

 

• Part (4) is correct: to review the annual targets states the purpose of the meeting.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the contrast that SSC sets year after year: ‘The captain, as well as the players, is ready’ (singular) against ‘The captain and the players are ready’ (plural).

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The village healers scraped the bark of the neem tree for their medicines.
option_1: The bark of the watchdog echoed through the empty lane.
option_2: The bark of the birch peels away in thin papery sheets.
option_3: Elephants strip the bark from young saplings in the reserve.
option_4: The rough bark of the oak was covered with moss.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The bark of the watchdog echoed through the empty lane.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but an entirely different meaning. In the given sentence, bark means the tough outer covering of a tree. (पेड़ की छाल)

 

• In Option 1, bark means the sharp explosive cry of a dog. (कुत्ते का भौंकना) That is a wholly different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The two words even reached English by different routes — the covering of a tree from Old Norse, the cry of a dog from Old English beorcan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: the bark of the birch — the covering of a tree; identical in meaning to the highlighted word.

 

• Option 3: strip the bark from saplings — again the covering of a tree.

 

• Option 4: the rough bark of the oak — the same sense once more.

 

NOTE

 

• A third sense of the same word exists — bark as a small sailing ship (also spelt barque) — and the idiom ‘his bark is worse than his bite’ means that a person sounds far more severe than he actually is.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

He was seen entering the store room by the security guard.
option_1: The security guard saw him entering the store room.
option_2: The security guard had seen him to enter the store room.
option_3: The security guard was seeing him enter the store room.
option_4: He entered the store room and was seen by the security guard.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The security guard saw him entering the store room.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The agent introduced by by — the security guard — becomes the subject of the active sentence, and the passive subject he becomes the object him.

 

• The passive verb was seen is in the simple past, so the active verb is saw. The participle entering describes the action observed and is carried over unchanged.
◦ Active: The security guard saw him entering the store room.

 

• Verbs of perception — see, hear, watch, notice, observe — take either the bare infinitive (saw him enter) or the -ing form (saw him entering) in the active. In the passive, however, only the to-infinitive is possible: He was seen to enter the room.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 changes the tense to the past perfect and uses to enter after an active verb of perception, which is ungrammatical.

 

• Option 3 turns the verb into the past continuous, altering the sense of a single completed observation.

 

• Option 4 splits the sentence into two clauses and leaves half of it in the passive voice.

 

NOTE

 

• The same asymmetry governs causatives: They made him work late (active, bare infinitive) but He was made to work late (passive, to-infinitive).

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Specialisation is the engine of modern knowledge and, increasingly, its cage. The division of intellectual labour has allowed enquiry to advance to a depth no generalist could ever reach; yet the same division steadily narrows the field within which a specialist can even recognise a question as intelligible. The expert grows fluent in a dialect that fewer and fewer colleagues can follow, and the fluency itself becomes deceptive — a command of vocabulary is mistaken, by speaker and listener alike, for a command of the subject. A discipline that has refined its instruments beyond the reach of its neighbours may discover that it has purchased precision at the cost of relevance. The difficulty is not merely one of communication. Every field trains its members to notice certain kinds of evidence and to dismiss the rest as noise; and those habits of attention, invisible to the very people who hold them, decide in advance what will be allowed to count as a finding. When two disciplines examine the same object — a river, an epidemic, a city — they may produce accounts that do not so much disagree as fail to meet. The economist’s model and the ecologist’s survey describe worlds that never quite touch. Nor is technology the remedy it promises to be. Search tools deliver more literature than any scholar can read and, by ranking what is already heavily cited, quietly reinforce the very boundaries they were expected to dissolve. Interdisciplinary conferences produce goodwill far more reliably than they produce collaboration. What the work actually demands is a humbler and harder discipline: a willingness to be a novice in public, to hold one’s own framework at arm’s length, and to treat another field’s questions as worth answering before they are worth judging. The frontier of knowledge no longer lies only at the outer edge of each field; it lies in the untended ground between them.

 

What is the tone of the passage?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Critical.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Critical here means examining something carefully and pointing out its faults, not merely finding fault for its own sake. (आलोचनात्मक)

 

• The author concedes the achievement of specialisation in the very first line — it is the engine of modern knowledge — and then devotes the rest of the passage to its costs: the deceptive fluency, the habits of attention that decide findings in advance, the failure of technology, the emptiness of interdisciplinary goodwill. The judgement is measured but consistently unfavourable.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Celebratory would require praise; the single word of praise is immediately qualified by “and, increasingly, its cage”.

 

• Option 3: Whimsical suggests playful, fanciful writing, which the sustained seriousness of the passage rules out.

 

• Option 4: Indifferent would mean the author had no stake in the matter; the closing prescription shows otherwise.

 

NOTE

 

• Tone is judged from word choice, not subject matter. Words such as cage, deceptive, purchased precision at the cost of relevance and goodwill rather than collaboration fix the tone long before the argument ends.

The frontier of knowledge no longer lies only at the outer edge of each field; it lies in the untended ground between them.

 

Which of the following best illustrates a paradox mentioned in the passage?
option_1: Specialists now understand one another better than ever before
option_2: Search tools meant to dissolve disciplinary boundaries end up reinforcing them
option_3: Interdisciplinary conferences are never attended by specialists
option_4: Economists and ecologists study entirely different cities
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Search tools meant to dissolve disciplinary boundaries end up reinforcing them.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A paradox is a statement in which the outcome contradicts what was expected. The passage states that search tools, by ranking what is already heavily cited, quietly reinforce the very boundaries they were expected to dissolve — the expectation and the result point in opposite directions.

 

• The paragraph on technology is introduced with “Nor is technology the remedy it promises to be”, which announces the reversal in advance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the passage, which says the expert’s dialect can be followed by fewer and fewer colleagues.

 

• Option 3 overstates a remark about conferences producing goodwill rather than collaboration; nothing is said about attendance.

 

• Option 4 misreads the example: the two disciplines examine the same object and still fail to meet.

 

NOTE

 

• To locate a paradox, look for the signposts of reversal — yet, nor, however, expected to … but, and phrases such as at the cost of. The sentence containing one of these usually holds the answer.

The economist’s model and the ecologist’s survey describe worlds that never quite touch. Nor is technology the remedy it promises to be. Search tools deliver more literature than any scholar can read and, by ranking what is already heavily cited, quietly reinforce the very boundaries they were expected to dissolve. The frontier of knowledge no longer lies only at the outer edge of each field; it lies in the untended ground between them.

 

The phrase “a novice in public” most likely refers to:
option_1: Publishing one’s findings before they are complete
option_2: Being willing to appear a beginner openly while learning another field
option_3: Teaching beginners as part of one’s professional duties
option_4: Refusing to acquire expertise in any single field
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Being willing to appear a beginner openly while learning another field.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase occurs in the list of what genuine cross-disciplinary work demands, alongside holding one’s own framework at arm’s length and treating another field’s questions as worth answering before they are worth judging. All three describe an attitude of humility.

 

• A novice is a beginner; the addition of “in public” points to the discomfort of admitting ignorance in front of others, which is precisely why the author calls the discipline humbler and harder.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 concerns the timing of publication, which the passage never discusses.

 

• Option 3 takes novice to mean the people one teaches, reversing the sense — it is the expert who becomes the novice.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the passage, which values depth and objects only to the isolation that can accompany it.

 

NOTE

 

• A phrase in a list takes its colour from the items beside it. When asked what such a phrase means, read the whole list; the common idea running through it is the answer.

Every field trains its members to notice certain kinds of evidence and to dismiss the rest as noise; and those habits of attention, invisible to the very people who hold them, decide in advance what will be allowed to count as a finding. When two disciplines examine the same object — a river, an epidemic, a city — they may produce accounts that do not so much disagree as fail to meet. The economist’s model and the ecologist’s survey describe worlds that never quite touch. Nor is technology the remedy it promises to be. Search tools deliver more literature than any scholar can read and, by ranking what is already heavily cited, quietly reinforce the very boundaries they were expected to dissolve. Interdisciplinary conferences produce goodwill far more reliably than they produce collaboration. What the work actually demands is a humbler and harder discipline: a willingness to be a novice in public, to hold one’s own framework at arm’s length, and to treat another field’s questions as worth answering before they are worth judging. The frontier of knowledge no longer lies only at the outer edge of each field; it lies in the untended ground between them.

 

Why, according to the author, does technology fail to solve the problem?
option_1: It has made research literature far too expensive to obtain
option_2: It supplies more material than can be read and ranks it by existing citation, hardening old boundaries
option_3: It removes the need for specialists to learn a shared vocabulary
option_4: It prevents scholars from attending conferences in person
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It supplies more material than can be read and ranks it by existing citation, hardening old boundaries.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage gives two linked reasons: search tools deliver more literature than any scholar can read, and, by ranking what is already heavily cited, they push the reader back towards the established centre of a field.

 

• The effect is therefore the opposite of what was hoped — the boundaries technology was expected to dissolve are quietly reinforced.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 raises cost, which the passage nowhere mentions.

 

• Option 3 inverts the argument about specialist dialects.

 

• Option 4 misreads the remark about conferences, which concerns their results, not attendance.

 

NOTE

 

• When a question asks why something fails, the answer usually lies in the sentence immediately following the claim of failure. Here it follows “Nor is technology the remedy it promises to be.”

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Specialisation is the engine of modern knowledge and, increasingly, its cage. The division of intellectual labour has allowed enquiry to advance to a depth no generalist could ever reach; yet the same division steadily narrows the field within which a specialist can even recognise a question as intelligible. The expert grows fluent in a dialect that fewer and fewer colleagues can follow, and the fluency itself becomes deceptive — a command of vocabulary is mistaken, by speaker and listener alike, for a command of the subject. A discipline that has refined its instruments beyond the reach of its neighbours may discover that it has purchased precision at the cost of relevance. The difficulty is not merely one of communication. Every field trains its members to notice certain kinds of evidence and to dismiss the rest as noise; and those habits of attention, invisible to the very people who hold them, decide in advance what will be allowed to count as a finding. When two disciplines examine the same object — a river, an epidemic, a city — they may produce accounts that do not so much disagree as fail to meet. The economist’s model and the ecologist’s survey describe worlds that never quite touch. Nor is technology the remedy it promises to be. Search tools deliver more literature than any scholar can read and, by ranking what is already heavily cited, quietly reinforce the very boundaries they were expected to dissolve. Interdisciplinary conferences produce goodwill far more reliably than they produce collaboration. What the work actually demands is a humbler and harder discipline: a willingness to be a novice in public, to hold one’s own framework at arm’s length, and to treat another field’s questions as worth answering before they are worth judging. The frontier of knowledge no longer lies only at the outer edge of each field; it lies in the untended ground between them.

 

Which of the following metaphors best captures the overall argument of the passage?
option_1: A single road climbing steadily to one summit
option_2: A cluster of tall towers with no bridges between them
option_3: A mirror that reflects only the person looking into it
option_4: A library whose books have all been read
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A cluster of tall towers with no bridges between them.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage describes disciplines that have grown deep (the towers) but remain unconnected — accounts that do not so much disagree as fail to meet, and worlds that never quite touch. Height without connection is exactly the image required.

 

• The closing line completes the metaphor: the frontier lies in the untended ground between the fields — that is, in the space where the bridges are missing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 suggests a single, unified path to knowledge, which the passage denies.

 

• Option 3 would fit a passage about self-absorption in general, but it captures neither the depth nor the separation described here.

 

• Option 4 implies completed knowledge, whereas the passage speaks of a frontier still untended.

 

NOTE

 

• For metaphor questions, translate each option into a plain statement and test it against the thesis, not against a single sentence. The correct metaphor must account for both halves of the argument — here, depth and isolation.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

She availed the opportunity of meeting the visiting delegation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. availed herself of the opportunity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Avail is used reflexively in standard English: the structure is avail + oneself + of + something, meaning to make use of an opportunity or facility.
◦ Corrected: She availed herself of the opportunity of meeting the visiting delegation.
◦ Example: Candidates should avail themselves of the free coaching offered.

 

• Both parts of the pattern are compulsory — the reflexive pronoun (himself, herself, themselves) and the preposition of. Omitting either produces the error tested here.

 

• The reflexive pronoun must agree with the subject: He availed himself of …, They availed themselves of …

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 places the reflexive pronoun after of, reversing the order of the pattern.

 

• Option 3 retains the faulty structure and merely changes the tense.

 

• Option 4 attaches the pronoun to the end, where it makes no grammatical sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Other verbs that demand a reflexive pronoun: pride oneself on, absent oneself from, resign oneself to, acquit oneself well, enjoy oneself, apply oneself to, accustom oneself to.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The number of applicants for the post have increased sharply this year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. has increased.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The expression ‘the number of’ is singular, because the subject is the number itself — a single figure — and not the people counted. It therefore takes a singular verb.
◦ Corrected: The number of applicants for the post has increased sharply this year.

 

• Contrast this with ‘a number of’, which means many and takes a plural verb:
◦ The number of applicants has increased.
◦ A number of applicants have withdrawn.

 

• The plural noun applicants sits inside the prepositional phrase of applicants and can never govern the verb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the plural auxiliary have with a singular subject.

 

• Option 3 is plural and also changes the sense to an action still in progress.

 

• Option 4 turns the verb passive, which suggests that someone increased the number deliberately.

 

NOTE

 

• Similar singular expressions: the majority of the work is, the amount of, the quantity of, the total of. Similar plural expressions: a number of, a variety of, a couple of, plenty of.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said, “I may join the coaching class next month.”
option_1: He said that he may join the coaching class next month.
option_2: He said that he might join the coaching class the following month.
option_3: He said that he could join the coaching class the following month.
option_4: He said that he might have joined the coaching class next month.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He said that he might join the coaching class the following month.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb said is in the past, so the modal must be back-shifted: may → might. The pronoun I becomes he, and the time expression next month becomes the following month.
◦ Indirect: He said that he might join the coaching class the following month.

 

• The modal might here preserves the original sense of possibility; it is not a change of meaning but the ordinary sequence of tenses.

 

• Note that some modals do not change at all — would, could, might, should, ought to, must (in the sense of obligation) — because they have no further past form.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves both the modal and the time expression unchanged.

 

• Option 3 replaces may with could, which expresses ability or permission rather than possibility.

 

• Option 4 uses might have joined, which reports an action that never took place.

 

NOTE

 

• Modal back-shift at a glance: can → could, may → might, will → would, shall → should, must → must / had to.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

She told her brother that she would help him with his project the next day.
option_1: “I would help you with your project the next day,” she told her brother.
option_2: “I will help him with his project tomorrow,” she told her brother.
option_3: “I will help you with your project tomorrow,” she told her brother.
option_4: “She will help you with your project tomorrow,” she told her brother.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. “I will help you with your project tomorrow,” she told her brother.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Converting to direct speech means undoing every change made in reporting:
◦ the modal returns — would → will;
◦ the pronouns return — she → I (the speaker) and him/his → you/your (the person addressed);
◦ the time expression returns — the next day → tomorrow;
◦ the connective that is dropped and inverted commas are supplied.

 

• Direct: “I will help you with your project tomorrow,” she told her brother.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the reported forms would and the next day inside the quotation.

 

• Option 2 changes the time expression but leaves him and his, which no speaker would use while addressing that very person.

 

• Option 4 puts she inside the quotation, so the speaker appears to be talking about somebody else.

 

NOTE

 

• The safest method is to work backwards through the four elements in order: reporting verb → pronouns → tense/modal → adverbs of time and place. Missing any one of them is what the wrong options are designed to catch.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. When the new bypass opened, the shopkeepers of the old market braced themselves for ruin.

 

A. Traffic that had once crawled past their shutters now sped around the town altogether.

 

B. Within a year, however, the emptied street had become something the town had never possessed — a place in which to walk.

 

C. Small cafés and bookstalls took over the premises the workshops had left behind.

 

D. Rents fell steeply and half the older businesses moved out to the highway.

 

S2. The bypass had not killed the market; it had merely changed what the market was for.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A-D-B-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – D – B – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from fear → cause → decline → reversal → new life → verdict.

 

• S1 states the fear of ruin.
◦ A gives the immediate cause — the traffic now bypasses the market altogether.
◦ D records the decline that follows from A: rents fall and businesses leave.
◦ B marks the turn with “Within a year, however”, and the word emptied looks back to the departures in D.
◦ C describes what filled the space — the premises the workshops had left behind — which can only be the premises vacated in D, so C must come after both D and B.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (D-A-B-C) places the fall in rents before the diversion of traffic that caused it.

 

• Option 3 (A-B-D-C) allows the street to be described as emptied before anyone has moved out.

 

• Option 4 (D-B-A-C) separates the cause in A from its effect and leaves the reversal unexplained.

 

NOTE

 

• A contrast word such as however, yet, nevertheless never begins the chain; it marks the point at which the situation already described is reversed, and so belongs in the middle of the sequence.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The word ‘salary’ carries within it a fragment of Roman economic history.

 

A. Whether they were handed the salt itself or an allowance with which to buy it is still argued over by historians.

 

B. It descends from salarium, a payment connected with salt, then a costly and strictly controlled commodity.

 

C. Either way, the association between pay and salt has outlived the empire that created it.

 

D. Roman soldiers, posted far from the coastal pans, needed a dependable supply of it.

 

S2. A man who does not deserve his wages is still said, two thousand years later, not to be worth his salt.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from claim → derivation → circumstance → doubt → conclusion.

 

• S1 makes the claim that the word preserves a piece of Roman history.
◦ B supplies the derivation — salarium, a payment connected with salt — and the pronoun It at its head refers directly back to the word in S1.
◦ D explains the circumstance: soldiers far from the salt pans needed a supply of it, the pronoun pointing back to the salt named in B.
◦ A raises the doubt about how exactly they were paid.
◦ C begins with “Either way”, which can only follow the two alternatives set out in A, and closes the argument before S2 supplies the surviving idiom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-A-D-C) raises the doubt about payment before the soldiers have been introduced.

 

• Option 2 (D-B-A-C) opens with it before the salt has been mentioned at all.

 

• Option 4 (B-D-C-A) places “Either way” before the alternatives it refers to.

 

NOTE

 

• Phrases such as “Either way”, “In either case”, “Whichever it was” always follow a sentence offering two possibilities. Spot the pair first, and the position of such a sentence is fixed.
